newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Horlick still battling for MGAM deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Horlick still battling for MGAM deal.

text.p: Former Morgan Grenfell star fund manager Nicola Horlick on Tuesday stepped up attempts to be reinstated or compensated by the firm from which she resigned in a blaze of publicity last week but her former employers appeared deaf to her pleas.

Despite indications that discussions were taking place between her lawyers Herbert Smith & Co and legal representatives of parent bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, a DMG spokesman denied there had been further contact.
The bank is sticking firmly to its guns in the row with the 35 year-old mother of five, one of London's most prominent fund managers.

It says Horlick, having been promoted to the rank of managing director, was suspended just days later for allegedly trying to lead a virtual takeover of MGAM's pension fund business by Dutch bank ABN AMRO and then resigned her position.
DMG's line is that she will not be reinstated and that there will be no compensation because she had resigned her position.
DMG's parent, the mighty Deutsche Bank, also said late Monday that it did not expect to go to court with Horlick.

Deutsche board member Rolf Bruer, who is poised to take over the helm of Deutsche in May from Hilmar Kopper, said:"The facts are clear. Mrs Horlick inflicted damage on the bank with her attempt to poach staff and then resigned."
But Horlick's lawyer John Farr said late on Monday that discussions were taking place and that he might be meeting his client later on Tuesday.
"I have talked to their (DMG's) lawyers," Farr said. "There have been further discussions and that's the way it rests at the moment."
Farr said on Monday Horlick would consider legal action against DMG if no settlement could be reached but her adviser said on Tuesday that it was too early to consider the courts.

Horlick continues to deny allegations that she was leading a breakaway group. On leaving Farr's office on Monday evening she said, "I'm still convinced that what I'm saying is true, I wasn't about to lead anyone astray."
Meanwhile, differing versions of what led up to Horlick's suspension continued to trickle out.

British newspaper reports said ABN AMRO was involved with Horlick in planning to fund a management buyout of the 18 billion pounds ($30 billion) pension fund business which Horlick headed. They said ABN ARMO planned to recruit Horlick and her team and then to offer to buy the residue from a stunned Morgan Grenfell for a reported sum of 385 million pounds.
ABN AMRO declined to comment on the latest reports but has already denied having tried to poach Horlick and her team.

But on Tuesday the Dutch bank acknowledged it would be interested in buying a large British fund manager and its global asset management director Jan Vroegop told Reuters it would like to make "big steps" in London funds management.

Horlick's colleagues were reported to have been unconvinced by the merits of ABN's alleged plan to poach the team, not least because one of the team's key aims had been to have Horlick promoted to a more influential position within MGAM. Once this happened it removed a key complaint against top management.

MGAM has had a troubled time since the sacking of MGAM fund manager Peter Young last September after irregularities came to light in three of the group's funds, hitting staff morale and also rattling clients.
Young has denied any criminal activity and is being investigated by Britain's Serious Fraud Office.
Since Young's departure Horlick had played a key role in reassuring MGAM's British pension fund clients and the firm has intensifed these efforts since Horlick's resignation.

So far no clients have withdrawn their business from MGAM as a result of the Horlick affair however several major clients have expressed their concern and said they would be reviewing their relationship with the firm. ($1=.6021 Pound)
